name: Battles of Lexington and Concord

phases.title: The militia stand on Lexington Common
phases.text: About 80 Lexington militiamen formed up on the Common in plain sight, but not across the road to Concord. Pitcairn's advance guard entered Lexington, with Smith's remaining companies further down the road.

phases.title: The Regulars charge and the militia disperse
phases.text: After shots were fired, of which the accounts disagree on the first, the Regulars charged with bayonets. Eight Lexington men were killed and ten wounded, and the militia fell back.

phases.title: The Regulars search Concord
phases.text: Smith reformed the column and marched to Concord, where he divided it to search for supplies. Four companies under Captain Parsons went beyond the North Bridge, while Laurie's companies guarded it. Barrett's militia watched from a hill to the north.

phases.title: The fight at the North Bridge
phases.text: Barrett's militia advanced on the bridge and exchanged fire with Laurie's companies, who broke and fled to the grenadiers coming from the town. This isolated the four companies at the farm.

phases.title: The column leaves Concord and is hit on the road
phases.text: Parsons' companies returned to the town and the Regulars marched east. Militia converged on the road and the British charged up Brooks Hill, but the colonists held it and inflicted heavy casualties on the attackers.

phases.title: Percy's brigade rescues the column at Lexington
phases.text: Near the Lexington line Parker's men, some bandaged, ambushed the column from a hill, and Smith was wounded. Percy's brigade arrived with artillery and fired at extreme range, dispersing the pursuing militia.

phases.title: Percy's column fights its way to Charlestown
phases.text: The combined column set out with flankers on both sides and the rearguard rotated. Militia fought it all along the road, notably at Jason Russell's farm in Menotomy. Percy turned onto a track to Charlestown, and the circle of fire was broken.

note: The plan shows the whole running fight along the road from Lexington to Concord and back to Charlestown, not a single field. Distances are only roughly to scale, and the accounts do not say which side of the road each hill and farm lay on; those are placed by judgement. The accounts differ on who fired the first shot at Lexington; the plan does not decide it.
